newsitem.title: USA: St Louis Fed VP concerned about rural U.S. banks.
newsitem.headline: St Louis Fed VP concerned about rural U.S. banks.

text.p: Local banks in rural areas may have to seek regulatory relief to survive the advent of nationwide branch banking, St Louis Fed Vice President Alton Gilbert said on Thursday.

Federal law permits large banks to open nationwide branches next year. Gilbert addressed a conference at which local bankers complained they will be obliged to follow the Community Reinvestment Act, a series of initiatives to promote local lending, while a branch of a large bank in their community would not.

"This is neither right nor fair," said Kenneth Guenther, executive vice president of the Independent Bankers Association of America. He said that without regulatory relief, community banks could be put at a disadvantage.

Guenther urged local bankers to take an active role in legislation expected in the new Congress to repeal the Glass- Steagall and Bank Holding Company laws. He also called for action to aid community bank liquidity, perhaps through the Farm Credit System or Federal Home Loan Bank.
Gilbert and Guenther addressed the Kansas Federal Reserve Bank's "Financing Rural America" conference.
Gilbert said his study of statewide branch banking suggested that large banks could become the dominant banking organizations in rural America if nationwide branch banking follows the same trend.

It is hard to tell whether large-scale branch banking will help or hinder rural economic activity, he said. But if credit becomes more constrained in rural areas, local banks could become more important and could argue for regulatory relief, he said.
In a paper, Gilbert examined the role of large bank organizations in 21 states, 12 that allowed statewide branch banking and nine that allowed multibank holding companies.

In states with statewide branch banking, the large banks tended to be the dominant organization in rural counties. In California, for instance, the five largest banks had offices in 16 of the 18 rural counties studied and held more than 75 percent of the deposits in most of those counties.
If state experience is a reliable indicator for nationwide branching, he said, "large banking organizations will be the dominant organizations in rural counties" throughout the U.S.

Studies were unclear whether rural residents benefitted when a big bank opened a branch near them, Gilbert said. Some studies show subsidiaries were less active than local banks in agricultural lending. But others say statewide branching spurred the rate of state economic growth.
